fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "A single scripture written in the constellations", "body": "Chance Garton opens with David Warner Mathisen, whose site starmythworld.com collects years of work arguing that the world's myths are one scripture written in the constellations. Mathisen traces his own start to childhood nights watching stars with his father and to H.A. Rey, the Curious George illustrator whose 1952 book The Stars, A New Way to See Them redrew the constellation outlines. That outlining system, he says, is what makes the mythical connections visible, and without it the same stars hide them. Chance has begun with Star Myths of the World Volume Four, on Norse mythology."}, {"title": "The jailed preacher who said it two centuries ago", "body": "Mathisen insists he is not the first to notice this. He points to Plato hinting at it, to Christmas carols full of stars and heavenly host, and above all to Robert Taylor, a preacher of the late 1700s and early 1800s who drew large crowds in London, spent three years in jail for it, and left behind The Devil's Pulpit and a separate set of astronomico theological lectures, both searchable on archive.org. Mathisen thinks the term astrotheology comes from Taylor. Chance adds Godfrey Higgins and Anacalypsis, which argues the same universal system from the etymology side."}, {"title": "Why the knowledge disappeared and who benefited", "body": "Much of the hour asks why this vanished. Mathisen ties Taylor to the French free thinkers, the revolution of 1789 and the American break of 1776, when Benjamin Franklin pushed to outlaw inherited titles and dismantle feudalism, a system held in place not only by castles and armed men but by a literalist church teaching that lords ruled by divine decree. Chance argues the ecclesiastical order was the machinery that funneled land and wealth upward. Mathisen cites economist Michael Hudson on how oligarchy struck back, and compares the star system to kung fu, powerful and good but capable of being hijacked."}, {"title": "Ships, bows, dragons and the ark of the waters", "body": "Chance drives a long riff on language. The ship of state leads to the constellation Argo and its prow, to bow as both arc and weapon, to arche and archon meaning head and ruler. He notes the Viking drakkar, the Greek dracon, and the Chinese dragon boat whose word for dragon is long, links he thinks nobody arranged on purpose. Mathisen answers that myths everywhere are handed down in verse, stylized measured language built on metaphor and double meaning. Both then read the ark, from Moses to Perseus to Sargon of Akkad, as the boat of the female generative power carrying a seed."}, {"title": "Myths as maps back to the buried self", "body": "Mathisen's answer to why we need myths at all is psychological. Drawing on Peter Levine, Gabor Mate and Richard Schwartz, he describes trauma as separation from self, an unconscious survival move a small child makes and then forgets. The myths dramatize exactly that, he says, in babies set adrift in arks, in Osiris cut into fourteen pieces, in Jesus in the tomb, in Inanna stripped and hung in the underworld, and every one of them comes back. Chance connects this to his sound healing work, which he says can locate stuck energy in the biofield, and Mathisen ends on John Michell's Twelve Tribe Nations."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: The stellar scholar and prolific author David Warner Mathisen joins InnerVerse to discuss the ancient universal system, codified in the stars above. Join us as we explore the origins of all myths, religious texts, and perhaps even some star stories that are disguised as "ancient history."
fields.Intro Paragraph 2: In the Plus+ Extension we discuss the Hercules constellation, chaos, and the storm gods of the world. We also get into a deep speculation about what the technology of star myth might mean about the nature of the universe, and the possibility of great cycles in which consciousness expands and contracts.

fields.Plus Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Hercules as a worldwide storm god figure", "body": "David Warner Mathisen argues that gods and heroes linked to the constellation Hercules share recognizable traits across cultures, including a square head, a protruding tongue, a powerful weapon and command of thunder and wind. He points to Heracles, Tiki, the Gorgons, Thor and the Maya Hurricane as examples. Chance Garton adds the view that the same stars can be read as a churning vortex, so the storm god and the creator god overlap. Both treat the matches as evidence of a shared older system rather than coincidence."}, {"title": "The swastika, Whirlwinds and the Big Dipper", "body": "Chance Garton shows images of Hercules as a square with four arms and floats the idea that this shape may be the root of the swastika. David Warner Mathisen agrees that ancient Greek pottery places swastikas beside Gorgons posed like Hercules, and he links the sign to whirlwinds and divine wind. He is careful to say he is not certain, argues the Big Dipper explanation lacks matching ancient artwork, and stresses the symbol was later hijacked by oppressors."}, {"title": "Does technology cost us our inner knowing", "body": "Chance Garton wonders whether humanity has devolved, suggesting that as language, writing and technology externalized knowledge, an innate ability to know directly from the cosmos faded, perhaps in a cycle that swings back and forth. David Warner Mathisen pushes back, arguing the myths praise community and division of labor and that tools are neutral, so the morality of their use falls on people. Both agree that mind to mind connection across distance deserves serious attention."}, {"title": "Specialization, the Cyclops and know thyself", "body": "David Warner Mathisen reads the Odyssey's Cyclops, who live apart, build no ships and answer to no one, as a warning against a society with no shared work. He argues the Delphic call to know thyself means recognizing each person's different mix of talents, and that balance, nothing to excess, applies to division of labor. Chance Garton raises the cost of specialization, suggesting people forget skills once convenience takes over, and the two meet on moderation."}, {"title": "Wordplay, metaphor and seeking divine wisdom", "body": "Chance Garton defends playing with language, the green language, as a way to engage both brain hemispheres and to read life like a dream, even when scholars would not accept it. David Warner Mathisen prefers claims he can prove, such as the lotus in the sky, while granting that speculation is worthwhile. He ties wisdom to Solomon's request, Delphi and the guidance of Hermes and Athena, and both describe myth and poetry as connection between things that seem unrelated."}]
